summary.text: In vascular plants, roots are the organs that anchor the plant and take in water and nutrients.
Their primary functions are anchorage, uptake of water and dissolved minerals, and conduction of these resources to the shoot.
Roots also store reserves, as in sweet potato and carrot, and form partnerships such as mycorrhizae and nitrogen-fixing nodules.

facts.label: Main jobs
facts.value: Anchorage, water and mineral uptake, conduction to the shoot

facts.label: Where they grow
facts.value: Mostly below the soil, but some grow above ground

facts.label: Mangrove roots
facts.value: Pneumatophores allow gas exchange where soil oxygen is limited

items.prompt: A storm bends a field of crops, but the plants with vigorous root systems stay upright. Which root job is at work?

options.label: Holding the plant in the soil against mechanical forces
Making plant hormones for the shoot
Taking in gases from the air
Storing food for the next season

items.explain: Roots fix the plant in the substrate and resist mechanical forces, which is why vigorous root systems matter for crop stability.

items.prompt: A mangrove stands in waterlogged mud with little oxygen, yet its roots can still respire. How?

options.label: Its roots store oxygen for the whole season
Its roots take oxygen up through the xylem
Specialised structures such as pneumatophores allow gas exchange
Its leaves push air down into the mud

items.explain: Pneumatophores and aerial roots permit gas exchange where soil oxygen is limited, enabling respiration in mangroves.

items.prompt: After a dormant season, a plant regrows using carbohydrates kept underground. Which root function supplied them?

options.label: Anchorage
Storage of reserves
Uptake of minerals
Vegetative propagation

items.explain: Many roots accumulate carbohydrates and water that support perennial growth or regrowth after dormancy.

items.prompt: Water taken in by root hairs has to reach the shoot. How does it get there?

options.label: Through the xylem
Through the root hairs alone
Through the pneumatophores
Through the nodules

items.explain: Root epidermal cells and root hairs take up soil water, which is then conducted to the shoot via the xylem.

items.prompt: A gardener puts a cutting in water and new roots sprout at its base. What does this ability let many species do?

options.label: Fix nitrogen from the air
Survive without any water uptake
Grow taller without any support
Reproduce asexually and regenerate after damage

items.explain: Adventitious rooting on stems, nodes or cuttings allows many species to reproduce asexually and regenerate after damage.

items.prompt: A plant in poor soil does better because its roots form mutualisms with other organisms. What do these partnerships give the plant?

options.label: Less need for any water at all
A stronger hold against wind only
Much greater nutrient acquisition and stress tolerance
Extra sugars made in the roots by photosynthesis

items.explain: Mutualisms such as mycorrhizae and nitrogen-fixing nodules greatly increase nutrient acquisition and stress tolerance.

paragraphs.heading: What roots are
paragraphs.text: In vascular plants, roots are the organs that hold the plant in place and bring water and nutrients into its body. Doing this lets a plant grow taller and faster. Most roots sit under the soil. Some, though, are aerial or aerating roots that grow up above the ground, or above water.

paragraphs.heading: Holding on
paragraphs.text: Roots have three main jobs: anchoring the plant, absorbing water with its dissolved minerals, and passing those supplies up to the shoot. As anchors, they fix the plant in the ground and resist the push of wind and moving water. A vigorous root system is essential to keeping crops stable.

paragraphs.heading: Drinking from the soil
paragraphs.text: The outer cells of the root, called epidermal cells, and fine root hairs take in soil water and the ions dissolved in it. From there the water travels to the shoot through the xylem. Along with water and minerals, roots send some compounds they have made to the shoot through their vascular tissues, the xylem and phloem. How deep and how wide the roots spread decides which layers of soil they can draw from.

paragraphs.heading: Pantries and messengers
paragraphs.text: Many roots, such as fleshy taproots and tuberous roots, stock up on carbohydrates and water. These reserves keep a plant going year after year or help it grow back after dormancy. Sweet potato and carrot are familiar examples. Roots also make and adjust plant hormones such as cytokinins, which shape how the shoot develops and how the whole plant works.

paragraphs.heading: Partners and breathing room
paragraphs.text: Roots form partnerships called mutualisms, such as mycorrhizae and nitrogen-fixing nodules. These links greatly boost how much nutrient the plant gathers and how well it copes with stress, and they also reshape the roots themselves. Where the soil holds little oxygen, special structures like pneumatophores and aerial roots let gases in and out. That lets mangroves and other hydrophytes keep respiring.

paragraphs.heading: Props and new plants
paragraphs.text: Adventitious roots and brace or prop roots, seen in maize, some mangroves and the banyan, give a plant extra support and steadiness. Adventitious roots can form on stems, nodes or cuttings, and this lets many species reproduce asexually and recover after damage. Horticulture makes wide use of this.
